They color our perception of information, often subconsciously, leading us to favor certain ideas or data while dismissing others that don't align with our preconceived notions. Secondly, availability heuristic occurs when individuals rely on easily accessible examples or memories to make judgments. This can skew understanding, as it doesn't necessarily reflect the true probability or significance of an event or idea.

Thirdly, cognitive dissonance—the discomfort felt when holding contradictory beliefs—can prompt individuals to rationalize or ignore facts that contradict their worldview, preventing them from updating their knowledge.

Lastly, cultural or societal biases can shape the questions we ask, the research we conduct, and the interpretations we give to findings. This can result in overlooking important aspects of a topic or reinforcing existing inequalities.

In summary, biases can limit our objectivity, narrow our perspectives, and distort our understanding of the world. To pursue knowledge effectively, it is crucial to recognize and mitigate the influence of these biases
